documents.title: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline Pheochromocytoma and Paraganglioma

chunks.content: Graphical abstract INTRODUCTION Pheochromocytomas, which are now categorized as adrenal paragangliomas (PPGL) and PPGL are rare neuroendocrine tumors arising from the adrenal medulla and the paraganglia of the autonomic nervous system, respectively, with diverse clinical behaviors ranging from benign to highly aggressive forms [ - ]. Accurate prognostication remains a challenge due to the heterogeneous nature of these tumors and the lack of universally accepted histopathological grading systems [ - ]. The Pheochromocytoma of the Adrenal Gland Scaled Score (PASS) has been proposed to stratify the risk of malignancy and adverse clinical outcomes [ , ]. However, limitations such as inter-observer variability and inconsistent predictive performance have been reported, raising concerns about its clinical utility [ - ]. The PASS, originally developed by Thompson, incorporates multiple histopathological parameters but lacks quantitative standards for each, leading to variability in interpretation and application across institutions [ , - ]. Previous research has demonstrated that the PASS, despite its modest overall performance, maintains a high negative predictive value (NPV), suggesting a potential role as a screening tool [ , - ]. Given these challenges, there is a need to refine prognostic models for PPGL to improve reproducibility and predictive accuracy. Recent efforts to develop a simplified scoring system, focusing on key histopathological features with the strongest associations to adverse events, have shown promise in reducing inter-observer variability and enhancing prognostic performance [ , , - ]. This multicenter study aims to evaluate the prognostic significance of the PASS across five tertiary referral centers in Korea, assess inter-institutional variability, and validate the utility of simplified PASS scoring systems for risk stratification in PPGL patients. MATERIALS AND METHODS Study cohort and data collection Five tertiary referral centers in Korea participated in this multi center study investigating the prognostic factors for paragangliomas. The participating institutions were Seoul National University Hospital (SNUH), Seoul National University Bundang Hospital (SNUBH), Samsung Medical Center (SMC), Seoul St. Mary’s Hospital, and Severance Hospital. All data were fully anonymized and merged prior to analysis, so that investigators were blinded to the identity of the contributing institutions. A total of 1,523 patients diagnosed with PPGL from 2007 to 2020 in 5 hospitals were initially identified. Among these, three cases of gangliocytic paraganglioma and two cases of cauda equina paraganglioma were excluded from the cohort, as these entities are currently classified as composite gangliocytoma/neuroma and neuroendocrine tumor, and cauda equina neuroendocrine tumor, respectively, according to the latest World Health Organization (WHO) classification of endocrine and neuroendocrine tumors [ ]. Therefore, the final study cohort comprised 1,518 patients. Of the total cohort, PASS information was available in 1,079 cases. Definition of clinical outcomes Adverse events were defined as the presence of recurrence, metastasis, or multifocality. Recurrence was defined as tumor relapsing in the vicinity of the operative bed. Metastasis was defined as pathologically or radiologically confirmed tumor spread to sites outside the operative bed, specifically bone and lymph nodes [ , - ]. Multifocality was defined as the presence of additional tumors, excluding bone or lymph node, detected at the time of pathological diagnosis. Recurrence-free survival (RFS) was defined as the interval from the date of surgery to the most recent follow-up or the time when an adverse event occurred. Statistical analysis All statistical analyses were performed using R Software (R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria). Continuous variables were compared using analysis of variance (ANOVA), and categorical variables were analyzed with Fisher’s exact test. Survival outcomes were evaluated with Kaplan-Meier plots and the log-rank test in the subset of 363 cases with available RFS data. Univariable and multivariable Cox proportional hazards models were used to assess prognostic factors for RFS in these 363 cases. For adverse event outcomes, univariable and multivariable logistic regression analyses were conducted separately for patients with available PASS data (n = 1,079). Pair-wise Delong test was performed for comparison of area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) among five institutes. A two-sided p-value < .05 was considered statistically significant. RESULTS Baseline characteristics The baseline characteristics of the study cohort are summarized in . Mean age, sex distribution, tumor size, tumor localization, PASS, and disease status are presented for each hospital. Significant differences in mean age were observed among the institutes (ANOVA, p < .05); specifically, hospital D had a higher mean age compared to hospitals A and E. PASS also differed significantly among groups, with hospital A exhibiting higher scores than the other hospitals. For tumor localization, cases of paraganglioma in which the localization could not be identified in the electronic medical records were classified as unknown. PASS as prognostic indicator of adverse events Univariable and multivariable logistic regression analyses were performed to evaluate the odds ratios of each variable in the total cohort of 1,518 cases ( ). In univariable analysis, all variables except sex were statistically significant. However, in multivariable analysis, only age (per 10 years) (odds ratio [OR], 0.68; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.60 to 0.76; p < .001) and PASS category (intermediate risk [4–5]: OR, 2.05; 95% CI, 1.22 to 3.35; high risk (≥6): OR, 4.83; 95% CI, 3.12 to 7.50; p < .001) remained significant. Kaplan-Meier survival analyses were conducted for the 363 cases with available survival data. Survival curves were stratified by age (≤45 years vs. >45 years), sex, tumor localization (adrenal vs. extra-adrenal), tumor size (≤5.0 cm vs. >5.0 cm), and PASS category (low risk [≤3], intermediate risk [4–5], high risk [≥6]), as shown in . According to the log-rank test, significant differences in survival were observed for age and PASS score categories (all p < .001). In contrast, sex, tumor localization, and tumor size did not show statistically significant differences in survival. Cox proportional hazards regression analysis for disease-free survival indicated that all variables except sex were statistically significant in univariable analysis ( ). In multivariable analysis, age (per 10 years) (hazard ratio [HR], 0.71; 95% CI, 0.60 to 0.83; p < .001), localization (extra-adrenal: HR, 2.96; 95% CI, 1.71 to 5.14; p < .001), and PASS category (intermediate risk [4–5]: HR, 6.12; 95% CI, 2.3 to 16.3; high risk [≥6]: HR, 12.5; 95% CI, 5.49 to 28.5; p < .001) remained significant. Both multivariable logistic regression and Cox proportional hazards analyses demonstrated the prognostic significance of histopathological grading systems. The screening role of PASS: high NPV offsets modest predictive performance The predictive performance of the PASS score for adverse events was further evaluated using logistic regression-based receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis, as summarized in . The PASS demonstrated an AUC of 0.673, sensitivity of 0.511, specificity of 0.836, NPV of 0.885, and positive predictive value (PPV) of 0.409. The grid plot demonstrated a low incidence of adverse events in the low-risk group (53 of 720 patients [7.4%]) and a comparatively higher incidence in both the intermediate-risk group (32 of 169 patients [18.9%]) and the high-risk group (59 of 190 patients [31.1%]) ( ). Previous studies, including a recent meta-analysis, have also suggested that the high NPV of the PASS supports its utility as a screening tool for risk stratification in pheochromocytoma and PPGL [ ]. Our findings are consistent with these prior reports, indicating that while the predictive accuracy of the PASS system alone may be suboptimal, its high NPV renders it a valuable prognostic grading system. Inter-observer variability of the PASS The PASS is composed of multiple histopathological parameters, many of which lack quantitative or objective criteria. As a result, concerns have been raised regarding inter-observer variability in its application [ , ]. To further assess this issue, the predictive performance of the PASS for adverse events was evaluated across five different hospitals. The AUC for each institution was as follows: hospital A, 0.698; hospital B, 0.513; hospital C, 0.727; hospital D, 0.665; and hospital E, 0.687 ( ). Pairwise DeLong tests revealed statistically significant differences in AUC between hospital A and hospital B, as well as between hospital B and hospital C (p < .05) ( ). These findings indirectly demonstrate inter-observer variability in the application of the PASS score, or at the very least, highlight discrepancies in its predictive performance among different institutions. The distribution of positive cases for each PASS parameter in the adverse event group revealed that nuclear pleomorphism, capsular invasion, and nuclear hyperchromasia were the most frequently observed features ( ). Notably, when the proportion of each PASS parameter was further analyzed across the four participating institutes, substantial variation was observed in several parameters—including capsular invasion and nuclear hyperchromasia ( ). These findings not only identify which parameters are most commonly seen in the adverse event group but also suggest inter-observer variability in PASS parameter assessment among institutions, underscoring the limitation of applying PASS. These findings not only identify which parameters are most commonly seen in the adverse event group but also suggest inter-observer variability in PASS parameter assessment among institutions, underscoring the limitation of applying PASS. Multivariable analysis of PASS parameters and development of the Simple PASS Multivariable logistic regression analysis was conducted on 560 samples with available PASS parameter scoring to evaluate the association between individual PASS parameters and adverse events ( ). Among the PASS parameters, only confluent necrosis, tumor cell spindling, and mitotic figures (>3 per 10 high-power fields [HPF] were statistically significant. Specifically, confluent necrosis was associated with an OR of 3.38 (95% CI, 1.76 to 6.52; p < .001), tumor cell spindling with an OR of 1.89 (95% CI, 1.13 to 3.12; p =.016), and mitotic figures (>3/10 HPF) with an OR of 2.00 (95% CI, 1.10 to 3.58; p = .023). These three parameters were included in the 3-factor Simple PASS, while vascular invasion—despite its marginal significance (OR, 1.64; 95% CI, 0.94 to 2.83; p = .080)—was added to the 4-factor Simple PASS. This decision took into account that other scoring systems, such as GAPP (grading of adrenal pheochromocytoma and paraganglioma) and COPPS (COmposite Pheochromocytoma/paraganglioma Prognostic Score), also incorporate vascular invasion as a parameter [ , ]. Based on these odds ratios, the 3-factor Simple PASS was developed by assigning 3 points to confluent necrosis, 2 points to spindling, and 2 points to increased mitotic figures. ROC curve analysis identified an optimal cut-off of 1 point according to the Youden index, indicating that the presence of any single parameter was sufficient to classify a case as high-risk. When high risk was defined as the presence of one or more parameters, subsequent ROC analysis yielded an AUC of 0.646, sensitivity of 0.519, specificity of 0.740, NPV of 0.837, and PPV of 0.374 ( ). Furthermore, the 4-factor Simple PASS was created by adding vascular invasion, assigned one point, to the original 3-factor model. Using the same optimal cut-off of 1 point, as determined by the Youden index, ROC analysis demonstrated an AUC of 0.701, sensitivity of 0.497, specificity of 0.891, NPV of 0.938, and PPV of 0.374 ( ). Notably, the 4-factor Simple PASS showed improved AUC, specificity, and NPV compared to the original PASS. When comparing the performance of the simplified PASS systems between hospitals A and B, the difference in AUC was less pronounced than that observed with the original PASS in both simplified models ( , ). Importantly, the difference in AUC between the two hospitals for the simplified PASS was not statistically significant (DeLong test p = .658 for the 3-factor model and .465 for the 4-factor model), in contrast to the significant difference observed with the original PASS score (p = .005). These findings suggest that applying the simplified PASS reduces inter-observer variability. DISCUSSION The clinical utility of the PASS system for risk stratification in PPGL has been demonstrated in numerous previous studies, supporting their roles as prognostic indicators for adverse clinical outcomes [ - , , ]. In the present multicenter study, we validated the prognostic impact of PASS using what is, to the best of our knowledge, the largest cohort to date. Our results align with prior research, confirming that PASS is associated with adverse events and RFS. Specifically, multivariable logistic regression analysis in our cohort of 1,518 cases revealed that age and PASS were independent predictors of adverse events, with age per 10 years having an OR of 0.68 (95% CI, 0.60 to 0.76; p < .001) and high-risk PASS scores (≥6) conferring an OR of 4.83 (95% CI, 3.12 to 7.50; p < .001). ROC curve analysis showed that the PASS score had an AUC of 0.673, sensitivity of 0.511, specificity of 0.836, and a notably high NPV of 0.885. These findings are consistent with previous meta-analyses and large-scale studies, which have emphasized the high NPV of the PASS as a screening tool, despite its modest overall discriminative performance [ , - ]. The association between younger age and adverse events may be explained by the fact that adverse events often involve multiplicity, and younger patients are more likely to carry germline mutations and exhibit multiplicity [ - ]. Further studies are warranted to precisely define adverse events using genetic profiles, to distinguish true adverse events from mere multiplicity. Further studies are warranted to precisely define adverse events using genetic profiles, to distinguish true adverse events from mere multiplicity. A major advantage of the PASS system is its simplicity and cost-effectiveness, as it can be assessed solely on histopathological grounds without the need for additional molecular or clinical data [ , ]. However, the PASS system incorporates numerous parameters, many of which lack quantitative definitions, leading to substantial inter-observer variability [ - ]. This issue has been widely recognized in the literature, and our multicenter analysis provides further robust evidence that both the diagnostic validity and interpretative application of the PASS score are subject to considerable variability across institutions. Specifically, diagnostic performance as measured by AUC ranged from 0.513 to 0.727 among the five participating centers, with statistically significant pairwise differences observed in certain comparisons. Furthermore, our detailed exploration of individual PASS parameters demonstrated substantial heterogeneity in their assessment: for instance, capsular invasion and nuclear hyperchromasia showed pronounced discrepancies in the proportion of positive cases among centers. Such inter-institutional differences are likely attributable to variability in pathologists’ interpretation and implementation of the PASS criteria. These results underscore the persistent challenge of inter-observer variability. In response to the limitations of the PASS, several alternative grading systems have been introduced, including the GAPP and other composite models [ - ]. However, each of these systems has its own constraints, such as limited validation, reliance on additional clinical or biochemical data, or continued subjectivity in parameter assessment. Despite these limitations, the PASS remains a valuable screening tool due to its high NPV, and ease of use based solely on histopathology [ ]. To address inter-observer variability and improve the prognostic performance of PASS, we conducted multivariable analysis to identify the parameters most strongly associated with adverse events. Based on these results and previous studies, confluent necrosis, tumor cell spindling, and increased mitotic figures (>3/10 HPF) were incorporated into a 3-factor simplified PASS scoring system, while vascular invasion was additionally included to develop a 4-factor simplified PASS. Notably, the 4-factor model—where single presence of vascular invasion, necrosis, spindling and increased mitosis can be assigned as high-risk group—demonstrated improved AUC (0.701), specificity (0.891), and NPV (0.938) compared to the original PASS score, despite the reduced number of parameters. Furthermore, when comparing the performance of both simplified PASS systems between hospitals A and B, the difference in AUC was not statistically significant, suggesting reduced inter-observer variability relative to the original PASS system. This study has several limitations. First, we did not review pathological slides or revise the initially diagnosed PASS to avoid retrospective bias, as the main goal of this study was to evaluate how well the PASS system performs in real-world practice with respect to diagnostic accuracy and inter-observer variability. During data collection, we realized that the absence of a refined consensus on the definitions of each parameter might have contributed to inter-observer variability, underscoring the high demand for precise and standardized definitions of each factor. As a multicenter retrospective analysis, the completeness and consistency of data collection may be suboptimal. While the relationship between PASS score and adverse events was the primary focus, survival data and detailed PASS parameter information was limited, resulting in smaller sample sizes (n = 560) for some analyses. Furthermore, we did not directly assess inter-observer agreement by having multiple pathologists independently review the same slides; rather, we inferred variability indirectly by comparing AUCs for adverse event prediction across institutions. Future studies should incorporate direct inter-observer concordance assessments to more precisely quantify variability. Another limitation concerns the definition of adverse events. Given that PPGL can arise anywhere along the paraganglionic system, distinguishing between multifocality, metastasis, and recurrence can be challenging, and these categories may overlap biologically [ , ]. We included multifocal tumors as adverse events but recognize that their biological behavior may differ from truly metastatic or recurrent tumors, potentially diminishing the predictive power of the PASS [ , ]. Additionally, previous studies suggest patients with germline mutations are more prone to multifocal PPGL, and immunohistochemistry (IHC) for S-100 and SOX-10 can be used to distinguish metastasis from multifocal tumors [ , - ]. Taken together, future research should incorporate genetic data and additional IHC study to distinguish multifocal cases from metastasis and refine the definition of adverse events accordingly. chunks.content: INTRODUCTION Primary aldosteronism is a common, under-recognized cause of secondary hypertension and is present in approximately 5–10% of all hypertensive patients [ , ]. Compared with essential hypertension (EHT), primary aldosteronism is associated with greater cardiovascular risk and target-organ damage, partly attributed to mineralocorticoid receptor–mediated inflammation, fibrosis, and oxidative stress beyond blood-pressure load [ , ]. Cardiac remodeling is a salient downstream consequence of renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system (RAAS) dysregulation. Patients with primary aldosteronism more often show left ventricular hypertrophy and myocardial fibrosis, often out of proportion to blood pressure; targeted treatment can partially reverse these changes [ ]. Left ventricular mass index (LVMI) is a robust marker of structural remodeling, whereas excess LVMI (eLVMI) quantifies left ventricular mass beyond that predicted by hemodynamic load, capturing maladaptive remodeling associated with adverse outcomes [ ]. Aging strongly shapes morbidity and mortality, but chronological age incompletely reflects inter-individual biological aging [ ]. The Gompertz law–based biological age (GOLD BioAge) model, derived from routine clinical biomarkers – offers a practical estimate of biological age [ ]; GOLD BioAgeDiff (BioAge–chronological age) predicts morbidity and mortality in general populations [ ]. Whether RAAS perturbations in primary aldosteronism are associated with accelerated biological aging, and whether this aging burden tracks cardiac structural remodeling remain unclear [ , ]. We hypothesized that elevated plasma aldosterone concentration (PAC), suppressed plasma renin activity (PRA), and a higher aldosterone-to-renin ratio (ARR) are associated with higher GOLD BioAgeDiff, which correlates with greater LVMI and eLVMI. METHODS Data sources This study is part of the Study on Primary Aldosteronism in Nanchang (NPAS), which was registered at Chinese Clinical Trial Registry (ChiCTR2200057297; https://www.chictr.org.cn/showproj.html?proj=133752 ). NPAS is an inpatient hypertension screening cohort established in 2017. The protocol was approved by the Biomedical Research Ethics Committee of the Second Affiliated Hospital of Nanchang University (approval number: 2022-05) and complied with the Declaration of Helsinki; prospective participants provided written informed consent, and retrospective data were de-identified before analysis. Study design, setting, and participants We conducted a retrospective cross-sectional analysis of hypertensive inpatients undergoing standardized evaluation for secondary hypertension at the Second Affiliated Hospital of Nanchang University (Nanchang, China). Clinical information from these routine screenings was curated into the NPAS database. Participants were classified into two groups based on their final diagnosis. The primary aldosteronism group consisted of consecutive patients diagnosed with primary aldosteronism and hospitalized between October 2017 and November 2022. The EHT group was drawn from patients hospitalized for screening between January 2019 and June 2019, in whom secondary causes were excluded. For the primary analysis, patients were excluded if they had missing data on key variables [age, serum creatinine (Scr), plasma glucose (Glu), mean corpuscular volume (MCV), red cell distribution width (RDW), serum albumin (Alb), alkaline phosphatase (ALP), lymphocyte percentage (Lym%), white blood cell count (WBC), and gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT), ARR, or postcaptopril PAC)], had a diagnosis of secondary hypertension other than primary aldosteronism, such as renovascular hypertension due to renal artery stenosis, renal hypertension due to renal parenchymal disease, pheochromocytoma, Cushing syndrome, obstructive sleep apnea, and gestational hypertension. or presented with extreme GOLD BioAge values (1.5 × interquartile range). For echocardiographic analyses, we additionally excluded patients without echocardiography. Diagnosis of primary aldosteronism The diagnosis of primary aldosteronism was made according to the Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline [ ], as previously described in our published work [ ]. Briefly, prior to admission, Patients stopped ARR-interfering medications or switched to verapamil and/or terazosin for 2–4 weeks. An ARR greater than 30 [(ng/dl)/(ng/ml/h)] prompted confirmatory testing (captopril challenge or saline infusion) to diagnose primary aldosteronism. Diagnosis of essential hypertension EHT was defined by office SBP at least 140 mmHg and/or DBP 90 mmHg on repeated inpatient measurements or a documented hypertension history with current treatment [ ], after excluding secondary causes through standardized work-up. Primary aldosteronism was excluded by ARR 30 or less under standardized medication preparation or by negative confirmatory testing when ARR was elevated [ ]. In addition, all secondary causes of hypertension were excluded through the standardized inpatient work-up as described above. Exclusion relied on history and physical examination, routine laboratory testing including renal function and urinalysis, endocrine assays when appropriate, and imaging or functional testing as clinically indicated. The final EHT diagnosis was determined by the treating physicians. PRA was derived from angiotensin I generation during incubation (4 versus 37 °C), and ARR was calculated as PAC/PRA. PRA was derived from angiotensin I generation during incubation (4 versus 37 °C), and ARR was calculated as PAC/PRA. For the primary aldosteronism screening test, samples for PAC and PRA were collected after subjects had been in a sitting or standing position for at least 2 h. Clinical data and comorbidity information were obtained from the electronic medical record system and the hospital's central testing laboratory, including sex, age, height, weight, duration of hypertension, SBP, DBP, smoking history, alcohol consumption, MCV, RDW, Alb, ALP, Glu, Lym%, WBC, GGT, serum potassium, serum sodium, total cholesterol (TC), triglycerides, high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL-C), low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C), Scr, and estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR). Smoking history was defined as smoking more than one cigarette per day, at least 1 year, or 18 packs per year. Alcohol drinking history was defined as on average, drinking alcohol at least two times a week for more than 1 year. Comorbidities were identified based on discharge diagnoses determined by specialist physicians in accordance with standard clinical guidelines. Outcome The primary outcome was GOLD BioAgeDiff, defined as the difference between the GOLD BioAge and chronological age. GOLD BioAge was calculated using the GOLD BioAge model [ ]: GOLD BioAge = chronological age+ ∑(β i × Biomarker i ) + β 0 (β 0 = −53.6287), where biomarkers were Scr, Glu, MCV, RDW, Alb, ALP, Lym%, WBC, and GGT. GOLD BioAgeDiff was defined as GOLD BioAge − chronological age. The secondary outcomes were LVMI and eLVMI. Doppler echocardiography was used to evaluate the cardiac structure as described previously [ ]. Echocardiography was performed by experienced sonographers blinded to diagnosis using standardized measurements. Two-dimensional and two-dimensionally guided M-mode images were recorded from standardized views. Left ventricular internal diameter in diastole (LVIDd), posterior wall thickness in diastole (PWTd), and interventricular septal thickness in diastole (SWTd) were measured and incorporated into the Devereux-modified formula to estimate left ventricular (LV) mass. LV mass was calculated by the formula: LV mass = 0.8 × {1.04[(LVIDd + PWTd + SWTd) 3 – (LVIDd) 3 ]} + 0.6 (g) [ ]. LVMI was calculated by dividing LV mass by body surface area (BSA). The body surface area was calculated as follow: BSA (m 2 ) = 0.0061 × height (cm) + 0.0128 × weight (kg) − 0.1529 [ ]. Stroke volume was derived using the Teichholz method [ ]. Stroke work was estimated as SBP (mmHg) × stroke volume (ml) × 0.0144 (g m), as previously described [ ]. As simultaneous SBP measurement immediately after echocardiography was not routinely available, we used admission SBP recorded within 48 h of the echocardiographic examination as a surrogate for systolic loading conditions. The predicted LVM was estimated by the equation derived previously: predicted LVM = 55.37 + 6.64 × height (m 2.7 ) + 0.64 × stroke work − 18.07 × sex (where sex was coded as male = 1 and female = 2) [ , ]. Predicted LVMI was then calculated as predicted LVM/BSA. The eLVMI was defined as measured LVMI − predicted LVMI [ ]. Statistical analysis Variables with at least 20% missing data were excluded from the analysis. For those with 20% or less missing values, missing data were imputed using multiple imputation, implemented through the mice package in R. Clinical characteristics were compared between patients with primary aldosteronism and those with EHT. Normally distributed data are presented as mean (SD) and compared using the Student's t test; nonnormally distributed data are summarized as median [IQR] and compared using the Wilcoxon rank-sum test. Categorical variables are described as counts (percentages) and compared using the χ 2 test or Fisher's exact test, as appropriate. ARR was log-transformed due to skewed distributions. Multivariable linear regression models were constructed for the primary analysis to evaluate the association of RAAS measures with GOLD BioAgeDiff, and for the secondary analysis to examine the relationship between GOLD BioAgeDiff and LVMI/eLVMI. Covariates were likewise selected a priori based upon clinical knowledge, previous literature, and data availability. For the primary analysis: Model 1 was unadjusted. Model 2 adjusted for sex, age, and BMI. Model 3 further adjusted for SBP, DBP, serum potassium, TC, triglycerides, HDL-C, LDL-C, cardiac insufficiency, peripheral vascular disease, coronary heart disease, atrial fibrillation, stroke, smoking, alcohol, and hypertension duration. For the secondary analysis: Model 1 was unadjusted. Model 2 adjusted for the full set of covariates used in primary Model 3. Model 3 was additionally adjusted for PAC, PRA, and log-ARR. Given the significant interaction between disease subtype (primary aldosteronism versus EHT) and ARR, subgroup analyses were restricted to the primary aldosteronism population. Mediation analyses were performed using nonparametric bootstrapping with 1000 iterations to examine whether GOLD BioAgeDiff mediates the association between ARR and eLVMI. These models were adjusted for sex, age, BMI, smoking, and alcohol. To compare mediation effects between primary aldosteronism and EHT, a bootstrap-based difference test with 5000 samples was conducted; significance was inferred if the 95% confidence interval (CI) of the average causal mediation effect (ACME) difference (Δ = ACME_PA − ACME_EHT) excluded zero [ ]. RESULTS Characteristics of the study population From October 2017 to November 2022, a total of 1053 patients diagnosed with primary aldosteronism were initially screened. In addition, 616 patients with EHT without primary aldosteronism, enrolled between January 2019 and June 2019, were included as a comparison group. After excluding 337 patients with missing data, 117 with concomitant secondary hypertension other than primary aldosteronism, and 14 with extreme GOLD BioAge values, 1201 patients were eligible for primary analysis, including 785 patients with primary aldosteronism and 416 patients with EHT. For the secondary analysis focused on echocardiographic outcomes, a further 92 patients without available echocardiography were excluded, yielding 1109 participants including 717 patients with primary aldosteronism and 392 patients with EHT (Fig. ). Among the 1201 patients included in the primary analysis, the mean age was 49.4 (11.0) years and 687 (57.2%) were men. The mean GOLD BioAge was 57 (13) years, and the mean GOLD BioAgeDiff was 7.6 (4.7) years. Compared with EHT, primary aldosteronism patients had the expected RAAS profile (lower PRA and higher PAC/ARR), were older with longer hypertension duration, and differed in electrolytes, lipids, and comorbidity patterns (Table ). Association between aldosterone, renin, and aldosterone-to-renin ratio and Gompertz law–based biological age difference In the overall cohort, RAAS indices were positively associated with GOLD BioAgeDiff (Table ). PhenoAge is an epigenetic biomarker calculated by weighting DNA methylation levels at 513 CpG sites [ ]. Primary aldosteronism features autonomous aldosterone excess with renin suppression, leading to chronic mineralocorticoid receptor activation [ ]. Mineralocorticoid receptor activation promotes oxidative stress and sterile inflammation, pro-fibrotic/vascular remodeling, and endothelial dysfunction with microvascular impairment across organs [ ]. Persistent mineralocorticoid receptor activation may induce mitochondrial dysfunction and reactive oxygen species generation, amplifying oxidative stress and inflammation [ ]. This cascade may also intersect with aging biology through Klotho-related pathways [ ]. Clinically, primary aldosteronism is associated with greater arterial stiffness and vascular aging than EHT, supporting blood pressure–independent pro-aging vascular effects of aldosterone [ ]. Furthermore, higher aldosterone exposure has also been associated with shorter leukocyte telomere length, consistent with aldosterone-related cellular senescence [ ]. Because these pathways affect inflammation, metabolism, and organ function, domains captured by the biomarkers in GOLD BioAge, mineralocorticoid receptor-mediated injury may manifest as a higher multisystem ‘aging burden’. This mechanism elucidates the phenomenon observed in our study: after fully adjusting for potential confounding factors, aldosterone-related indices remained independently and positively correlated with GOLD BioAgeDiff. Previous studies have provided strong evidence that accelerated biological aging aligns with structural target-organ damage, including cardiac remodeling. Recently, using UK Biobank data, Mao et al. showed that biological age acceleration, calculated via the the Klemera–Doubal and PhenoAge algorithms [ , ], was associated with adverse cardiac structure and function and a higher risk of incident heart failure; their Mendelian randomization analyses further suggested a potential causal contribution to cardiac remodeling [ ]. Higher ARR has been associated with arterial stiffness, LV hypertrophy, and atrial enlargement, partly independent of blood-pressure load [ ]. eLVMI represents LV mass beyond that predicted by body size and hemodynamic load, and may better reflect maladaptive, nonhemodynamic remodeling [ ]. In primary aldosteronism, GOLD BioAgeDiff was independently associated with LVMI and eLVMI, aligning with Mao et al. Mediation analyses further indicated that GOLD BioAgeDiff statistically accounted for part of the log-ARR–eLVMI association, though establishing causality and temporality requires longitudinal and interventional validation. In the subgroup analyses stratified by clinical characteristics, a nominal interaction was observed regarding diabetes status ( P for interaction = 0.036). The positive association between log-ARR and GOLD BioAgeDiff was prominent in participants without diabetes but was not statistically significant in those with concomitant diabetes. Diabetes is a strong driver of oxidative stress and inflammation and may produce a ‘ceiling effect’ that attenuates additional aldosterone-related aging signals [ , ]. Antidiabetic therapies such as metformin, SGLT2 inhibitors may also exert cardiometabolic benefits that modify RAAS-related injury signals [ – ]. Because subgroup analyses were exploratory and the diabetic subgroup was smaller, this interaction should be considered hypothesis-generating and requires confirmation. Methodologically, we used the complete GOLD BioAge model rather than Light BioAge because C-reactive protein required for the simplified model was not routinely measured [ ]. Additionally, the complete model includes immune cell, erythrocyte, and hepatobiliary indices that may better capture primary aldosteronism-related multisystem attrition [ , – ]. Because GOLD BioAge was developed in Western general populations, calibration in Chinese primary aldosteronism cohorts warrants evaluation. Nevertheless, applying the same algorithm across groups supports internal comparisons even if absolute biological age values shift systematically. GOLD BioAgeDiff is readily computed from routine laboratory indices and may serve as a quantitative phenotype of multisystem burden in primary aldosteronism. Its association with LVMI/eLVMI suggests potential utility for refined risk stratification and prioritizing cardiac assessment. chunks.content: Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 (MEN1) syndrome is a rare inherited tumor syndrome caused by germline pathogenic variants in the MEN1 gene coding the menin protein [ ]. Loss of heterozygosity and inactivation of both alleles of this gene predispose to MEN1 syndrome [ , ]. Menin is a scaffold chromatic adaptor protein, which interacts with various cellular proteins, including different nuclear receptors, epigenetic and cellular transcription factors, which are involved in gene regulation, DNA repair, and signaling transmission [ , ]. Menin has contradictory effects both as an oncogenic cofactor and as a tumor suppressor, depending on tissue type and cellular context [ , ]. In MEN1, abnormal structures and functions of menin are assumed to cause several changes in cellular functions and predispose to tumorigenesis [ ]. Clinically, MEN1 syndrome is typically characterized by an increased risk of neuroendocrine tumors (NETs) [ , , ]. These include parathyroid (pHPT), pituitary (PitNET), and pancreatic NETs (PNET), and less often other gastro-intestinal NETs. Other well-known but rarer tumors are thymic (TNET) and bronchopulmonary NETs [ , ]. Adrenal tumors (AdrT) are also present in more than 20% of MEN1 patients [ ]. In addition to neuroendocrine tumors, MEN1 syndrome has also been associated with more than 20 different neoplasms [ , ]. Several studies have reported an increased prevalence of breast cancer (BC) in MEN1 compared to the general population [ , ]. There are also reports of possible associations between MEN1 and thyroid [ , ] and urogenital cancers [ , ]. The aims of this study were (1) to evaluate the prevalence of BC, thyroid, and renal cancers (RC) previously reported in the literature to be associated with MEN1 in a registry-based retrospective Finnish MEN1 cohort and (2) to compare the findings with a representative local control population. Materials and methods Study population The data were collected at the Department of Endocrinology at Oulu University Hospital between November 1982 and December 2023 and all patients diagnosed with MEN1 during that period were included in the data collection ( n = 113, 45.1% males). The criteria for MEN1 diagnosis were applied according to previous guidelines [ , ]. All but one of our patients had a genetically confirmed diagnosis of MEN1. The patient without genetic MEN1 confirmation had pHPT and Zollinger-Ellison syndrome caused by a gastrinoma, meaning she had a clinical MEN1. The Oulu Project Elucidating Risk of Atherosclerosis (OPERA) was utilized as a control population. OPERA is an epidemiological cohort study originally designed for addressing cardiovascular disease (CVD) risk factors and clinical endpoints. Subjects ( n = 1045, 50% hypertensives, 50% males, age 40-62 years) were middle-aged hypertensives and their age- and sex-matched controls who were randomly selected between 1990-1993 from the local area, as previously described in detail [ ]. At baseline, participants were interviewed, examined, and tested in the University of Oulu research laboratory. Mortality and hospital events of the population have since been followed and the project is ongoing, with the latest major data collection in 2014. A flowchart presenting the study setup, and the analyses carried out is presented in the supplementary data (Fig. S1) [ ]. The study protocol was approved by the medical ethics committee of the North Ostrobothnia Hospital District and board reviews at Oulu University Hospital. Genetic studies of the MEN1 gene in the patients have been conducted as part of routine clinical work and counseling process. All participants of the OPERA cohort gave written informed consent. The Declaration of Helsinki 1975 was adhered to during the study. Clinical data and outcome classification Patient data, including clinical information such as sex, age at diagnosis of MEN1, family history, characteristics of tumors, their treatment, and outcomes, were obtained from both electronic medical records and clinical charts. Data on MEN1 patients were collected until the end of 2024, and on the control population until the end of 2014. The outcome “breast cancer” included all recorded BCs, including lobular carcinomas and ductal carcinomas. The outcome “thyroid cancer” included all recorded thyroid carcinomas. In both cohorts, all recorded thyroid cancers were papillary thyroid carcinomas (PTC). The outcome “renal cancer” (RC) included all recorded renal cell carcinomas (RCCs), including clear cell (CCRCC) and papillary (PRCC) carcinomas. Kaplan–Meier curves and Cox proportional hazards models were used to estimate the associations of MEN1 syndrome with the outcomes. A total of 33 women (3.2%) in the OPERA control cohort were diagnosed with BC compared to the 7 women in the MEN1 cohort (6.2%). In the OPERA control cohort, only 11 patients (1.1%) were diagnosed with PTC, a significantly lower prevalence than in the MEN1 cohort (6.2%) ( P < .001, Table S5) [ ]. The average age of PTC diagnosis in the control cohort was 49.6 years compared to 44.4 years in the MEN1 patients (Table S5) [ ]. In a crude Cox regression model, the HR for PTC in all MEN1 patients was 9.37 (3.59-24.41) ( ), 12.87 (3.70-45.03) in female MEN1 patients (Figure S2B) [ ], and 5.74 (1.14-28.8) in male MEN1 patients (Fig. S3A) [ ], respectively. The prevalent variant is 1 of our 2 founder mutations in Northern Finland [ ]. All these variants are supposed to result in a structurally and functionally altered menin protein. Curiously, there were no women with BC in our other large pedigree of MEN1 patients with the pathogenic variant c.1546dup in exon 10. Genetic testing is the only definitive confirmatory test for the diagnosis of MEN1. The traditional consensus has been that there are no genotype–phenotype correlations in genetically confirmed MEN1 [ ]. This conclusion has recently been challenged [ ], and our data suggest that in the case of some non-neuroendocrine cancers in MEN1, such correlations require further studies. Previous studies have reported BC with a mean age of diagnosis ranging from 48 to 56 years (median age of 45 years) in women with MEN1 [ , , , ]. In our study, the mean age of diagnosis of BC was 50 years in women with MEN1, lower than in female OPERA controls (62 years) or in the average Finnish female population (65 years) (FCR). BC was diagnosed in 11.5% of our MEN1 women (on average after 58 patient-years of follow-up) compared to 6.3% in female OPERA controls (on average after 73 patient-years of follow-up) and 8.3% to 11.2% in female population statistics from the Finnish Cancer Registry (70-80-year-old females) (FRC). The actual lifetime point prevalence in Finnish women to develop BC is 13.4% (FCR), and the incidence of BC in Finland has more than doubled from 1980 to the year 2020. In recent MEN1 cohorts, BC has been reported in 1.7% to 4.2% of MEN1 female patients [ , , ]. When compared to our local OPERA control cohort, the risk for developing BC in our MEN1 women was 3.79 (1.66-8.60), slightly higher than the previously reported risks from other cohorts, ranging from 2.31 to 2.83 [ ]. Our data suggest that BC can manifest in MEN1 women significantly earlier than in the average population, but data on the overall point prevalence of BC in MEN1 is currently lacking. The MEN1 gene codes for the protein is menin [ ]. It is widely expressed in various tissues and mostly expressed in the cell nucleus [ ]. It is a scaffold nuclear protein, which has interactions with more than 50 different nuclear proteins and functions through such interacting partners, especially with those which regulate and control transcription, epigenetic regulation, chromatin modifiers, DNA repair proteins, and cell signaling proteins [ ]. In typical NETs in MEN1, loss of menin and its tumor suppressive effects is thought to lead to the disruption of antiproliferative gene expression programs and to development of tumors [ , ]. In certain sporadic solid tumors such as BC, previous studies have found that menin can also have a pro-oncogenic effect and could be involved in BC pathogenesis [ , ]. Moreover, menin inhibitors have been tested as an adjunct to BC treatment [ , ]. Menin binds and is a coactivator for the nuclear protein estrogen receptor alpha (ERα) and regulates the expression of the gene ESR1 coding ERα, which are important drivers for BC tumorigenesis [ , ]. However, in sporadic non-MEN1 BC tumors, the role of menin in tumor pathogenesis is still uncertain and somewhat contradictory as both tumor promoter and tumor suppressive effects have been found [ , ]. In experimental MEN1 models, there are reports suggesting tumor suppressive effects of menin in the normal mammary epithelium [ , , ]. In BC women with MEN1, there are studies reporting a reduced expression of menin and a complete loss of heterozygosity of the MEN1 gene locus in breast tumor samples [ , ]. MEN1-BC tumors have been luminal-like, expressing ERα and/or progesterone

tumorigenesis [ , ]. However, in sporadic non-MEN1 BC tumors, the role of menin in tumor pathogenesis is still uncertain and somewhat contradictory as both tumor promoter and tumor suppressive effects have been found [ , ]. In experimental MEN1 models, there are reports suggesting tumor suppressive effects of menin in the normal mammary epithelium [ , , ]. In BC women with MEN1, there are studies reporting a reduced expression of menin and a complete loss of heterozygosity of the MEN1 gene locus in breast tumor samples [ , ]. MEN1-BC tumors have been luminal-like, expressing ERα and/or progesterone receptors, and have been histologically classified as invasive ductal carcinomas [ , ]. In our MEN1 women with BC, histologically, a lobular carcinoma was found in 1 and an invasive ductal carcinoma in 6 of them. In 2 women, the ductal carcinoma was aggressive and led to death. We had immunohistochemical data in 6 BC women with MEN1 and in 4 of them, BC was luminal B-like and luminal A-like in 2 of them. Although clinical and experimental data suggest an association of MEN1 syndrome and BC, the causal relationship remains uncertain [ , ]. Breast carcinogenesis is a multistep and complex process involving the accumulation of genetic alterations and is influenced by various environmental and hormonal risk factors [ , , , ]. In a Dutch study of MEN1 patients, various BC risk factors were analyzed and the findings indicated that the increased BC risk in MEN1 carriers was not related to other known BC risk factors or familial cancer history [ ]. About 5% to 10% of BC patients have inherited predisposition due to germline mutations of various BC risk genes [ ]. However, there are only 2 previous reports where BC risk genes have been studied in MEN1 patients [ , ]. To the best of our knowledge, our study is the only one in which known BC risk genes have been reported in MEN1 BC women. We analyzed an extensive panel of pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants of BC genes available in 6 out of 7 of our BC patients. We did not find highly penetrant BRCA1 and BRCA2 gene variants on them, which have been previously noted in case reports with simultaneous mutations in both MEN1 and BRCA2 or MEN1 and BRCA1 genes [ , ]. Also, other pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants in established BC genes were excluded in our patients. Previous large studies on genetic predisposition to BC have been unable to identify the MEN1 gene as a significant susceptibility gene in women with sporadic BC [ , ] or in women with hereditary BC [ , ], but MEN1 somatic mutations seem to have a driver role in women with metastatic BC [ ]. In conclusion, menin seems to have a role in BC tumorigenesis, but in BC of MEN1 patients, the pathogenesis is uncertain, and it is thought that menin alone is not sufficient for BC development [ ]. A higher prevalence of PTC was observed in our MEN1 patients (6.2%) compared to the OPERA controls (1.1%). Based on the Finnish Cancer Registry, the risk of developing PTC before the age of 70-80 years is 0.53% to 0.65% in the general population (FCR), indicating a similar prevalence as in our OPERA control cohort. The HR for PTC in our MEN1 patients was 9.37 (3.59-24.41) compared to the OPERA control cohort. Thus, our data suggest a higher prevalence of PTC in MEN1 patients compared to the general population. Although there are reports of a possible association between MEN1 and thyroid cancer [ , ], this relationship is thought to be incidental, possibly at least partially related to increased use of ultrasound examination [ ], and no loss of heterozygosity of the MEN1 locus has been observed in PTC tumor tissue in MEN1 patients [ ]. It has been concluded that there is no robust evidence from in vitro , animal, or human studies linking germline mutation of the MEN1 gene with the development of PTC [ , ]. Although we report an increased prevalence of PTC in MEN1 patients, this finding may be due to surveillance bias, and there is currently insufficient data to support a causal association between MEN1, and the occurrence of PTC and further studies are warranted. There are only a few previous studies on the possible association between MEN1 syndrome and RC [ , , ]. In our study with a small number of cases ( n = 5), a higher prevalence of RC was observed in the MEN1 patients (4.4%) compared to OPERA controls (1.2%). Based on the Finnish Cancer Registry, the risk of developing RC before the age of 70 to 80 years is 0.70% to 1.16% (FCR), suggesting a similar prevalence as in our OPERA

data to support a causal association between MEN1, and the occurrence of PTC and further studies are warranted. There are only a few previous studies on the possible association between MEN1 syndrome and RC [ , , ]. In our study with a small number of cases ( n = 5), a higher prevalence of RC was observed in the MEN1 patients (4.4%) compared to OPERA controls (1.2%). Based on the Finnish Cancer Registry, the risk of developing RC before the age of 70 to 80 years is 0.70% to 1.16% (FCR), suggesting a similar prevalence as in our OPERA control cohort. The HR for RC in our MEN1 patients was higher (7.80) compared to the OPERA control cohort with a longer follow-up period, suggesting a higher risk of RC in MEN1 patients compared to the general population. In a murine Men1 knockout model, heterozygous Men1 mutant mice did not develop RCs [ ]. Therefore, the data about the causal relationship between MEN1 and the occurrence of RC is uncertain. Although our data are consistent with current knowledge, several validity issues must be considered. We lack reliable information on socioeconomic and behavioral factors such as smoking and occupation, established cancer risk factors, and details on how certain cancers were initially diagnosed. It can also not be excluded that an unknown genetic factor closely linked to MEN1 could contribute to the increased risk of cancer types observed in our MEN1 patients. Our OPERA control cohort does not directly represent a general population cohort, is not designed for cancer incidence evaluation, and is not age-matched or matched for key clinical breast cancer (BC) risk factors relative to our study population. Because the OPERA cohort was not originally intended as a control cohort for MEN1, information on several important risk factors for our main outcomes is missing, and therefore, these factors could not be included in our regression models. For BC, however, the most important risk factors according to the World Health Organization are female sex and age. Both are accounted for in our models, as Cox regression inherently adjusts for age, and we performed separate analyses for men and women. In addition, we excluded the possibility of known high-risk BC genes such as BRCA1/2 in our MEN1 patients with BC, thereby addressing another major category of BC risk factors. Nevertheless, we lack information on reproductive history and postmenopausal hormone therapy in both the OPERA controls and the MEN1 cohort, meaning that residual confounding may partly explain the magnitude of the observed hazard ratios. The National Breast Cancer Screening Program in Finland was launched in 1987 for women aged 50 to 59 years and expanded to include women aged 50 to 69 years in 2007. Invitation coverage increased among women over 60 years of age until 2016, reaching over 95% in 2014. Thus, although the data collection periods for the OPERA cohort and the MEN1 cohort differ slightly, BC screening practices were largely comparable between the 2 groups. Moreover, the OPERA control cohort is slightly older and has a longer follow-up period than our MEN1 cohort, suggesting that if anything, the OPERA cohort should have a higher cancer prevalence than an age-matched control cohort. The OPERA population is also local, and the study period (1990s-2000s) aligns well with the time frame of most MEN1 patient data. Finally, our findings are further supported by comparisons with population-based data from the Finnish Cancer Registry. The demographics of our MEN1 cohort are similar to those reported in three large MEN1 cohorts from the Netherlands, Italy, and France [ , , ]. In summary, in this retrospective study, the risk of BC, PTC, and RC was higher in MEN1 patients compared with controls. Among women with MEN1 in whom other germline mutations in BC risk genes had been excluded, BC was diagnosed, on average, more than a decade earlier than in the control subjects. Our findings support the original Dutch and subsequent recommendations to initiate BC screening in women with MEN1 at the age of 40 years [ , ].

documents.title: ESE ENSAT Clinical Practice Guidelines on the Management of Adrenocortical Carcinoma

chunks.content: Background Adrenal incidentalomas are a common finding and affect approximately 2% of the general population and over 7% of those over the age of 70 ( ). On the other hand, ACCs are rare, comprising 0.4–4.0% of adrenal incidentalomas, with a female predilection and median age of 50–60 years at diagnosis ( , ). Spontaneous adrenal haemorrhage is also an uncommon clinical presentation; however, it can be associated with underlying adrenal tumours. Earlier and more frequent detection of both adrenal haemorrhage and malignancy is likely related to increased availability of improved imaging techniques; however, diagnosis based on clinical features remains difficult in the context of non-specific symptoms and signs. Case presentation A male patient in his fifties presented to the Emergency Department with sudden onset, atraumatic, severe left-sided flank pain and abdominal distension in the context of an adrenal incidentaloma found a year prior on CT imaging for acute appendicitis, with subsequent loss to follow-up. He had a background of obstructive sleep apnoea and untreated hypertension, with no personal or family history of malignancy and no regular medications. He was an ex-smoker with social alcohol intake. On examination, he had a measured blood pressure of 154/97 mmHg, weight of 97 kg and height of 174 cm (BMI 32 kg/m 2 ) with left-sided abdominal distension and flank tenderness without abdominal guarding. His other vital signs were within normal limits. Investigation Blood tests on admission showed a haemoglobin of 147 g/L (reference range (RR): 130–170), white cell count of 13.0 × 10 9 g/L (RR: 4.0–10.0) and estimated GFR of 87 mL/min/1.73 m 2 . Liver function tests and other electrolytes were within normal limits. CT renal tract and mesenteric angiogram imaging demonstrated a left retroperitoneal haematoma measuring 5.7 × 17 × 8 cm with evidence of active arterial extravasation from a well-defined left adrenal lesion measuring 59 × 53 × 52 mm ( ). CT abdomen and pelvic imaging performed a year preceding the presentation showed an incidental left adrenal body nodule measuring 17 × 13 mm, with a retrospective noted density of 40–50 Hounsfield units (HU) in the post-contrast phase ( ). Biochemical work-up for the adrenal lesion was performed ( ). There was no biochemical evidence of hormonal excess, with 24-h urine steroid metabolite testing revealing mildly elevated tetrahydrocortisone 12.6 μmol/day, RR: 2.5–12.0, with the remainder of urine steroid profile normal. There was no evidence of coagulopathy with normal coagulation markers and a negative antiphospholipid syndrome screen. The detailed results are presented in Treatment Initial management involved intravenous fluid resuscitation followed by successful embolisation of branches of the left suprarenal artery. Once stabilised, the patient was commenced on amlodipine for hypertension and discharged, with several subsequent re-presentations for pain management without evidence of active re-bleeding. Dedicated multiphase CT adrenal imaging completed 3 months after discharge showed a heterogeneous 39 × 53 × 43 mm left adrenal lesion with a density of 36 HU, absolute washout >50% and features of internal necrosis post-angio-embolisation. FDG-PET CT imaging was arranged to investigate for malignancy and demonstrated persistence of the adrenal mass, with maximum focal uptake SUV 4.5 thought to be confounded by the angio-embolisation and no evidence of extra-adrenal involvement ( ). Given the prolonged time to resolution of the haematoma and persistence of a large adrenal mass, the decision by a multidisciplinary team involving endocrinologists, endocrine surgeons, radiologists and pathologists was made to proceed to left laparoscopic adrenalectomy. This was completed 8 months after the initial presentation for haemorrhage, with no post-operative complications. Outcome and follow-up The patient had an R1 surgical resection, with visualised sub-capsular breach of necrotic appearing tissue and concerns for seeding into the adrenal bed. Histopathology showed adrenocortical neoplasm composed of polygonal cells arranged in sheets and trabeculae with variable areas of conventional and oncocytic appearance ( ). Areas of necrosis and capsular invasion were present ( ). Nuclear atypia was seen mostly in the oncocytic areas ( ). There were up to 6 mitoses per 50 high-power fields (HPFs) in the conventional areas. The Ki-67 proliferation index was estimated as 10%. Immunohistochemistry confirmed adrenal cortical differentiation with expression of SF-1, synaptophysin, inhibin A, melan A and calretinin (weak). The tumour was negative for GATA3, S100, chromogranin A, sox-10 and cytokeratin MNF 116. The tumour showed multiple atypical features, including three features within the Weiss criteria, which warranted a diagnosis of adrenocortical carcinoma (6 mitoses per 50 high-power fields, presence of necrosis and capsular invasion). Tumour staging was T2N0M0 with a corresponding European Network for the Study of Adrenal Tumors (ENSAT) stage II. Considering high-risk features on surgical resection and multidisciplinary input, the decision was made to offer adjuvant mitotane therapy and external beam radiotherapy (EBRT) to reduce the risk of local recurrence. Discussion Adrenal incidentalomas are adrenal masses detected on imaging completed for clinical indications other than suspected adrenal pathology ( ). Although 40–70% of cases are non-functioning adenomas, risk stratification and investigation are required to detect aetiologies requiring more active management. These include primary ACCs, phaeochromocytomas, functioning adenomas or metastases ( ). Clear guidelines exist for investigation and management, with a high number of included studies demonstrating loss to follow-up ( ). Spontaneous adrenal haemorrhage is uncommon, but often observed with adrenal tumours, sepsis, anticoagulation or coagulopathies. Overall, adrenal haemorrhage has an incidence of 0.14–1.8% in post-mortem studies with a likely increasing incidence in living patients given improved imaging techniques. However, it remains difficult to diagnose clinically due to non-specific features ( , ). Phaeochromocytomas were the most common underlying adrenal tumour (48%) in reported cases of adrenal haemorrhage, which require exclusion prior to surgical management due to the risk of precipitation of phaeochromocytoma crisis ( ). There is a notable difficulty differentiating phaeochromocytomas from ACCs on imaging alone. There is a paucity of data regarding resolution timeframes of spontaneous adrenal haemorrhage, attributed to incomplete follow-up imaging in reported cases. A retrospective study estimated a median time to resolution of 8 months without active intervention ( ). Time to resolution is likely dependent on the management approach and the underlying cause. Data on haemorrhage with associated adrenal masses is limited to case reports, with limited standardised guidelines on optimal diagnostic and management strategies. ACCs are rare, and 60% of cases are functional, in which hypercortisolism (50–70%), virilisation (20–30%), feminisation (5%) and mineralocorticoid excess (2–3%) are clinical features ( , ). The remainder are non-functional and present with mass effect symptoms or are discovered incidentally. Although CT imaging features, including tumour size ≥4 cm and density ≥20 HU, are associated with an increased risk of malignancy, no single imaging modality can confirm the diagnosis and histopathological confirmation is required ( , ). Urine steroid metabolomics have been shown to be a promising diagnostic adjunct, given the poor specificity of radiological features alone ( , ). There are established guidelines for management of ACC; however, recommendations are based on low-quality observational studies and expert consensus ( ). We present an uncommon case of an adrenal incidentaloma of unclear aetiology that was lost to follow-up and a subsequent re-presentation with spontaneous adrenal haemorrhage requiring urgent angio-embolisation. There were no symptoms or signs suggestive of phaeochromocytoma, nor any biochemical evidence of hormonal excess. In addition, there were no other features suggestive of metastatic disease on CT imaging. Adrenal haemorrhage was suspected to have originated from the pre-existing adrenal mass, in the absence of anticoagulation, coagulopathy or sepsis. The most anticipated lesion at this stage was a non-functioning adrenal adenoma given its overall incidence, with primary adrenal malignancy as an important differential. Surgical management for a persistent, non-functioning adrenal mass with slow resolution of the haematoma demonstrated a surprising finding of ACC on histopathology. Interestingly, urine steroid metabolomic testing completed after management of the haemorrhage only showed a mildly elevated tetrahydrocortisone level, with no other evidence of hormonal excess despite eventual histopathology confirming ACC. Although there are several other cases of adrenal haemorrhage reported in the literature, our case uniquely demonstrates haemorrhage associated with a pre-existing incidentaloma with the underlying aetiology being ACC. To our knowledge there are three other cases with the same features either under surveillance or having been lost to follow-up ( ). Our case mirrors that of existing studies with high attrition rates and stresses the need for judicious follow-up of adrenal incidentalomas. All adrenal nodules require exclusion of hormonal excess and dedicated adrenal imaging, with provision of clear plans to primary health practitioners if investigations are not completed in the inpatient setting. Historical autopsy data have shown a mortality rate of 15% with adrenal haemorrhage, often contributed to by the predisposing condition ( ). Fortunately, with our patient there was no significant haemodynamic instability, sepsis or adrenal insufficiency, the latter being more common in bilateral adrenal haemorrhage. Although current guidelines emphasise the need to assess for adrenal insufficiency in the context of bilateral adrenal haemorrhage and recommend further evaluation of adrenal nodules demonstrating imaging heterogeneity, they do not explicitly address the occurrence of adrenal haemorrhage in association with an adrenal nodule. Such cases should

investigations are not completed in the inpatient setting. Historical autopsy data have shown a mortality rate of 15% with adrenal haemorrhage, often contributed to by the predisposing condition ( ). Fortunately, with our patient there was no significant haemodynamic instability, sepsis or adrenal insufficiency, the latter being more common in bilateral adrenal haemorrhage. Although current guidelines emphasise the need to assess for adrenal insufficiency in the context of bilateral adrenal haemorrhage and recommend further evaluation of adrenal nodules demonstrating imaging heterogeneity, they do not explicitly address the occurrence of adrenal haemorrhage in association with an adrenal nodule. Such cases should prompt a heightened index of suspicion for underlying malignancy. Our case also highlights the requirement for multidisciplinary input in alignment with existing guidelines, in this case due to interval tumour growth and consideration of surgery. Although there was improvement of the haemorrhage on imaging at 4 months (median of 8 months in the literature with conservative management), this was thought to be slow to resolve given active angio-embolisation. Notably, FDG-PET CT imaging has utility in evaluating for metastatic disease and helping differentiate between adrenal haemorrhage and underlying malignancy, the former being non-FDG-avid. However, this can be confounded by inflammation and necrosis, present in our case’s lesion post angio-embolisation. Limitations of the case are a lack of long-term follow-up and aspects of the patient perspective; however, the focus of the report is to highlight adrenocortical carcinoma as a potential cause of adrenal haemorrhage. Adjuvant therapy for ACC is also controversial. Mitotane is the sole FDA-approved agent, with evidence of efficacy in prolonging disease-free survival limited to retrospective studies ( ). The only randomised controlled trial (ADUVIO) investigating this could not establish efficacy; however, given the good prognosis of low-risk patients with surveillance only, investigators recommended against its routine use for low-grade, localised ACC ( ). International consensus based on registry data and retrospective studies recommend consideration of adjuvant mitotane in high-risk disease. This includes tumour characteristics of a Ki-67 index greater than 10% or having many of the features that comprise the Weiss score, namely large size with necrotic components, capsular, lymphatic or vascular breach, high mitotic rate >5 per 50 HPFs and close surgical margins. The decision to use adjuvant mitotane in our case was based on capsular invasion of the tumour. Mitotane toxicities were discussed with the patient prior to commencement, including fatigue, nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, anorexia, skin rash, sedation and confusion. The patient was additionally counselled on important, potential adverse effects, including adrenal insufficiency and hepatic impairment, requiring initiation of glucocorticoid replacement and monitoring of liver function testing, respectively. Post-operative radiotherapy additionally could reduce the risk of recurrence and may increase disease-free and overall survival; however, evidence remains limited to retrospective studies. documents.title: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline Treatment of Cushing Syndrome

chunks.content: INTRODUCTION Cushing’s disease (CD) is a serious endocrine disorder characterized by chronic hypercortisolism due to an adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH)-secreting pituitary tumor [ ]. In Korea, a nationwide epidemiological study using the Health Insurance Review and Assessment Service database has provided important insights into the burden and demographic features of CD. Between January 2013 and December 2017, 584 new CD cases were identified, with an annual incidence of 2.3 cases per million and a prevalence of 9.3 cases per million population [ ]. Despite advances in diagnosis and treatment, CD continues to present clinical challenge [ ]. Even after achieving remission, patients remain at elevated risk for cardiovascular events, bone fractures, and persistent reductions in quality of life, and their mortality rates remain high [ ]. Therefore, early diagnosis and therapeutic intervention are crucial to improve outcomes. However, CD is often overlooked in daily clinical practice because of its rareness, leading to delays in diagnosis [ ]. It is thus essential to establish clear guidelines outlining when to suspect and how to diagnose CD. Several factors contribute to the diagnostic difficulty of CD, including its complex and variable clinical presentation and the challenges associated with localizing small pituitary tumors. Addressing these issues through standardized diagnosis criteria is critical to improving the clinical management and outcomes of patients with CD. Traditionally, hypercortisolism has been categorized into ACTH-dependent and ACTH-independent forms [ , ], and standardized diagnostic guidelines have been developed by various endocrine societies [ , ], including the Korean Endocrine Society (KES) [ ] and the Japan Endocrine Society (JES) ( ) [ ]. Despite shared pathophysiological principles, the KES and JES guidelines have notable differences, particularly in the selection of diagnostic tests, that reflect differences in healthcare systems, clinical practice patterns, and population-specific considerations. Therefore, a collaborative group from the KES and JES reviewed the current evidence and national guidelines to propose regionally relevant suggestions for the diagnosis of CD. METHODS A joint task force was assembled by the KES and JES in 2024, comprising endocrinologists and pituitary-adrenal specialists from both countries. Given the scarcity of high-quality comparative trials and meta-analytic evidence in the diagnostic evaluation of CD, particularly in original articles from both countries that demonstrate East Asian characteristics, and the substantial methodological heterogeneity between Korean and Japanese studies, applying a formal evidence-grading framework was not methodologically appropriate. Accordingly, the recommendations were formulated through multiple rounds of structured expert-consensus discussions involving specialists from both countries, consistent with international standards for harmonizing diagnostic guidelines. The task force conducted structured reviews of the existing the KES and JES guidelines, examined relevant literature, and engaged in multiple rounds of structured virtual and in-person discussions. Although the group did not apply formal evidence-grading tools, the recommendations reflect expert consensus and a synthesis of clinical experience across the two healthcare systems. This final document presents a narrative-based consensus intended to offer regionally relevant guidance for clinicians in East Asia. Each diagnostic topic is organized into a ‘Consensus statement,’ which summarizes the agreement reached by the KES–JES task force, and a ‘Clinical context,’ which outlines the supporting evidence, rationale, and country-specific considerations. This format aims to provide clear, practical guidance alongside necessary background information for clinical decision-making. CONSENSUS ON CLINICAL FEATURES OF CD Consensus statement The task force agrees that several clinical features are consistently observed in patients with CD and should raise clinical suspicion. Core manifestations commonly recognized across both the KES and JES guidelines include central obesity, moon face, proximal muscle weakness, purple striae, easy bruising, hypertension, glucose intolerance, menstrual irregularities, osteoporosis, and neuropsychiatric symptoms such as mood changes and cognitive impairment. Clinical context Symptoms listed only in the JES guidelines include thin skin, dorsocervical fat pads (buffalo hump), acne, peripheral edema, hyperpigmentation, and reduced growth velocity with obesity in children. Certain features such as facial plethora, dyslipidemia, delayed puberty, venous thromboembolism, immune dysfunction, and hypokalemia, are also noted as potentially relevant findings, particularly in East Asian populations. In contrast, the KES highlights symptoms such as facial plethora, weight gain, dyslipidemia, hypokalemia, delayed puberty, venous thromboembolism, cognitive dysfunction, and abnormalities in immune function. The JES categorizes clinical findings into specific and non-specific features and suggests that the presence of at least one from each category can support further diagnostic testing. The task force supports this approach in principle but emphasizes the need for clinician awareness that some patients might not spontaneously report even classic features [ ]. Thus, thorough clinical questioning and physical examination remain essential. The panel agrees that reddish-purple striae wider than 1 cm and disproportionate central adiposity—regardless of body mass index— are highly suggestive of CD. Although hyperpigmentation is typically associated with ACTH-dependent forms, it should not be confused with acanthosis nigricans related to insulin resistance, which may appear even in ACTH-independent adrenal disease [ ]. CONSENSUS ON DIAGNOSTIC EVALUATIONS

each category can support further diagnostic testing. The task force supports this approach in principle but emphasizes the need for clinician awareness that some patients might not spontaneously report even classic features [ ]. Thus, thorough clinical questioning and physical examination remain essential. The panel agrees that reddish-purple striae wider than 1 cm and disproportionate central adiposity—regardless of body mass index— are highly suggestive of CD. Although hyperpigmentation is typically associated with ACTH-dependent forms, it should not be confused with acanthosis nigricans related to insulin resistance, which may appear even in ACTH-independent adrenal disease [ ]. CONSENSUS ON DIAGNOSTIC EVALUATIONS FOR CD General diagnostic principles The task force agrees that no single diagnostic test provides definitive confirmation of CD. Therefore, a multimodal diagnostic strategy is essential to maximize diagnostic accuracy. Both the KES and JES recommend the use of at least two complementary screening tests to confirm hypercortisolism and reduce the risk of misdiagnosis. Test selection will depend on clinical presentation, institutional resources, and patient-specific factors. Biochemical diagnostic test Recommended initial tests The following tests are considered core first-line screening tools to evaluate endogenous hypercortisolism: • 24-hour urinary free cortisol (UFC) • Overnight dexamethasone suppression test (ODST) • Late-night salivary cortisol (LNSC) or midnight serum cortisol The initial step in CD diagnosis is to confirm cortisol excess through biochemical screening tests. KES recommends 24-UFC, LNSC, and 1-mg ODST as primary screening tests for suspected Cushing’s syndrome (CS). JES recommends measurements of early morning plasma ACTH and serum cortisol levels and the 24-UFC as the initial tests. An essential aspect of screening is identifying conditions that can lead to false-positive results in each test, including medications that increase corticosteroid-binding globulin (CBG) or enhance CYP3A4 activity and pseudo-CS, also known as non-neoplastic hypercortisolemia due to depression, severe weight loss or severe obesity, or excessive alcohol consumption. Conversely, cyclic CS can produce false-negative findings, further complicating the diagnostic process. Plasma ACTH and serum cortisol levels Consensus statement: Although morning ACTH levels are useful in differentiating ACTH-dependent CS from ACTH-independent CS, the task force notes that overlapping ACTH levels between CD and adrenal CS limit diagnostic specificity. • The KES guidelines place greater emphasis on suppression tests and diurnal variation rather than ACTH, as a primary screening tool, due to inconsistent findings in Korean studies. • The JES guidelines support the use of early morning plasma ACTH and serum cortisol as part of the initial evaluation, particularly when levels are normal or elevated in the presence of clinical suspicion. A flexible approach is endorsed, with ACTH levels interpreted alongside other biochemical and imaging data. 1. Clinical context In both Korea and Japan, serum cortisol is predominantly measured using automated immunoassay platforms, although the specific analyzers and reagents may vary among institutions, leading to modest inter-assay variability. However, these minor methodological differences do not sufficiently explain the discrepancies in cutoff values between the two national guidelines, which primarily reflect distinct diagnostic strategies rather than assay methodology. It should also be noted that mass spectrometry- based cortisol measurements have not yet been widely adopted in either country. Cortisol secretion follows a pulsatile pattern that is regulated by the circadian rhythm of ACTH. In healthy individuals, this diurnal variation is well established, with peak cortisol levels in the early morning and the lowest levels around midnight [ ]. The measurement of basal ACTH concentrations is particularly useful in distinguishing between pituitary-dependent (CD) and ACTH-independent CS [ ]. Because plasma ACTH is highly unstable, appropriate pre-analytical handling, including use of pre-chilled tubes, immediate placement on ice, and prompt centrifugation, is essential to prevent degradation and avoid falsely low values that may lead to diagnostic misclassification. In clinical practice, morning ACTH levels <10 pg/mL (2 pmol/L) with normal or high cortisol levels strongly suggest ACTH-independent CS, and ACTH levels >20 pg/mL (4 pmol/L) indicate ACTH-dependent CS [ ]. However, the KES guidelines do not explicitly include morning ACTH measurements as a required screening test for CS. Instead, the KES emphasizes biochemical suppression tests and diurnal cortisol variation for initial hypercortisolism detection. A Korean study found that plasma ACTH levels have significant overlap between CD and adrenal CS, which limits their diagnostic utility [ ]. That study reported that although low ACTH levels traditionally indicate adrenal CS, a considerable proportion of adrenal CS patients still had detectable ACTH levels (3.5 to 15.6 pmol/L), making differentiation unreliable. Another study conducted at a tertiary center in Korea analyzed baseline ACTH levels and diagnostic markers in patients with CD [ ]. That study found that preoperative ACTH levels did not differ significantly between macro-tumors (101.5±23.2 pg/mL) and microtumors (83.6±11.1 pg/mL, P =0.44), demonstrating a lack of correlation between ACTH levels and tumor size.
